# Where along the refusal opening does the adapter's circuit commit?

Offline structural analysis of the 30 `tc8192_refusal_first10` **adapter** attribution graphs (3 prompts x 10 positions). We analyse the adapter graph directly (not the overlay): within it, every transcoder feature attributes toward the SAME refusal token, so ranking features by |influence| is meaningful (in the overlay, base nodes attribute toward the base model's echo/gibberish target, so an adapter-vs-base influence share would be apples-to-oranges). For each traced refusal token we ask (a) which adapter features most influence it, (b) what context token each fires on -- the harmful request, the assistant-turn structure, or an already-emitted refusal token, and (c) which adapter features recur across positions/prompts. Feature ids match the viewer's `L?/F?` labels; to see what a feature detects, open it in the viewer (port 8054) for its top tokens + activating examples (§3-§4 list the top recurring ones to inspect).

## Findings (narrative)

**The refusal opening is driven mostly by turn-position features, not by reading the harmful request.** At almost every one of the 30 (prompt x position) graphs, the highest-influence adapter features toward the refusal token fire on the chat *scaffolding* -- `<start_of_turn>`, `user`, `model`, `\n` -- i.e. "I am the assistant, at the start of a reply to a user turn." The share of the top-8 features' influence that instead reads the harmful *request* content (e.g. the token "methamphetamine") is mostly 0-13% (Table 1, `req%`; figure left panel). So the circuit that emits "I cannot..." is largely a position/format-triggered response circuit, with harmful-content detection playing a smaller, prompt-specific role.

**The one clear content trigger is "bomb".** The pipe-bomb prompt (harm_116) is the exception: a layer-0 feature firing on the token " bomb" is a *top* feature at several positions (pos2 L0/F3059, pos6 L0/F3497) and request-reading reaches ~25% of top-8 influence at pos1 -- far more than "methamphetamine" (harm_125, intermittent) or "script" (harm_139, almost never). This matches the huge-adapter split, where weapons/CBRN are the most reliably refused categories.

**The refusal is already committed at position 0 ("I").** There is no position where a harmful-content feature suddenly switches the refusal on: the same turn-position features that drive "I" (pos0) drive "cannot", "provide", and the rest of the opening. A prompt-general set of adapter features recurs across all three prompts and almost all positions (Table 4: L0/F5489, L5/F6977, L6/F7928, L8/F3284, L9/F427, L12/F5446, ...), and these are exactly the scaffolding features. This is consistent with the prefill-flip result (instruct refuses at k=0, no "I" needed) and the huge-adapter split (the opener token is a *readout* of an already-made decision).

**Caveat -- these are labelled only by firing context, not verified as refusal-specific.** A feature firing on `<start_of_turn>` could be a generic response-start feature active for compliant answers too; distinguishing "refusal circuit" from "generic assistant-response circuit" requires contrasting against a COMPLIANCE graph (same feature active or not when the adapter complies). The huge-adapter compliance prompts (huge_adapter_refusal_split.md) are the natural contrast set. **One-sentence version:** across the first ten refusal tokens the adapter's refusal opening is driven overwhelmingly by chat-turn-position features (active from "I" onward, shared across prompts), with genuine harmful-content reading minor and prompt-specific (strongest for "bomb") -- so the refusal commits at the very first token as a position-triggered response, pending a compliance-graph contrast to confirm the features are refusal-specific.
